newsitem.title: USA: U.S. denies epidemic of aircraft near misses.
newsitem.headline: U.S. denies epidemic of aircraft near misses.

text.p: Officials on Tuesday denied there had been an epidemic of near misses in U.S. airways but said one recent incident needed more investigation and had already led to changes in military procedures.

The Feb. 5 incident in which a Nations Air Boeing 727 passenger jet made an evasive dive off New Jersey to avoid two nearby Air Force F-16s clearly raised potential safety concerns, National Transportation Safety Board officials said.

They said investigators were focusing on an apparent communications breakdown between military air traffic controllers and the pilots of the F-16 fighter jets and said they expected the military to announce procedural changes.

"The potential for very unfortunate results was clearly there," NTSB chairman Jim Hall told a news conference. "There clearly was miscommunication or a lack of communication between military air controllers and the flight of F16s.

"Our investigation continues. The military has implemented procedural changes," Hall said. He added that the safety board expected its own investigators to provide it with further safety recommendations within the next 10 days.

Hall noted that three other reported near misses between military and civilian planes had occurred on Feb. 7 over Delaware, Texas and New Mexico but investigations showed no one was in danger and they were "not in the same category as the incident involving the Nations Air aircraft."

"It seemed that we were experiencing an epidemic of incidents that seemed to raise concerns," he said, adding that that had not proven to be the case. He also said checks indicated there had been "relatively few instances of dangerous encounters between military and civilian aircraft."

In the Feb. 5 incident, one of the two F-16s trailed the Boeing 727 to "intercept" and identify it, officials said. The Nations Air pilot then manoeuvred violently in response to electronic cockpit instrument warnings indicating another plane was too close, causing two flight attendants and a passenger to be thrown to the cabin floor.
The Air National Guard commander, Maj. Gen. Donald Shepperd, said at the time "there was no imminent collision," and NTSB officials on Tuesday appeared to agree.

Greg Feith, the NTSB investigator on the case, said the investigation so far showed "there was no time when there was a conflict where there would have been a mid-air collision." But he said safety concerns arose all the same because of the evasive action by the Boeing 727. "The evasive action taken by that (Boeing 727) pilot may have been the only safety hazard."
Feith said the F-16 pilots had been alerted by military controllers that there was "traffic" in the area but had not been told that it was a civilian airliner passing through.

"From what we understand, that information should have been provided," he said. He could not say why one of the pilots decided to "intercept" the airliner to investigate instead of asking the military controller what it was.
